scrubmeta · Known limits

What scrubmeta Can't Do Yet

Our tool removes hidden personal details from files: names, GPS locations, dates, serial numbers. It does that job well. But it cannot do everything, and this page lists what it can't do. The small grey numbers point to the full list of limits, where each one is explained and measured.

16 November 2026
1

Some traces are part of the file itself

A camera's sensor leaves a pattern in every photo. No tool can remove it.

2

A cleaned file can still hint at the app that made it

It won't say who you are, but it can say "this came from an iPhone".

3

Some files are refused

If we can't clean a file safely, we stop and write nothing.

4

Some details stay on purpose

Removing them would break the file or change what it shows.

5

Some things are not tested yet

We don't claim anything we haven't checked.

The tool cleans at up to three strengths. The light clean removes the details and changes nothing else. The stronger cleans also rebuild the file so it looks like every other cleaned file, which hides the app that made it. Seven file types have stronger cleans: JPEG, PNG, MP3, FLAC, M4A, PDF and Word. Every other type has the light clean. #8, #43

Things no cleaning tool can remove

These traces are part of the picture, the sound or the text. Removing them would damage the file. Every tool has the same problem.

  • Camera noise. Every camera sensor leaves a faint, unique pattern in its photos. An expert can match a photo to the camera that took it. #5
  • Microphone and room sound. A recording carries the sound of the microphone and the room. The hum of the power grid can even help date it. #5
  • How a file was compressed. JPEG photos and MP3 songs carry a trace of the app that saved them. Only a stronger clean that re-saves the file removes it, and that costs a little quality. Some video apps write their name into the picture data itself. #1, #36
  • How a PDF was laid out. Where each letter sits on the page shows which program made the PDF. This stays even if the page is turned into a picture. #16, #17
  • How a Word document was built. The styles and settings a program chose still show which program wrote the document, even after the strongest clean. #25, #27
  • How a program was built. A program's code shows which compiler made it. The code is the program, so it can't change. #55
  • Text you can read. Words hidden under a black box in a PDF are still there. A name printed on a book's title page stays, and so does a user name a program prints when it crashes. We tell you where we find them, but we don't edit what you wrote. #13, #50, #63
  • A cleaned file looks cleaned. Someone can tell a cleaning tool was used. They just can't tell where the file came from. #9, #42

A cleaned file can still hint at the app that made it

We built the tool against an amateur investigator: someone who compares your file with many others using free tools. Even with every detail removed, the way a file is put together can point to the app that made it. It points to an app, not to you.

Most of the "Yes" rows have only the light clean so far. A stronger clean would fix many of them, and the measurements already say what it has to change.

Files we refuse to clean

When the tool can't clean a file safely, it stops and writes nothing. That is safer than handing back a file that still leaks, but you get no cleaned copy.

  • File types we don't handle yet: OpenDocument files, old Office files (.doc, .xls, .ppt), WAV, AIFF and Ogg audio, MKV, WebM and AVI videos, and .NET programs. #8, #54
  • Word documents with tracked changes or comments (at the light clean; the stronger cleans accept the changes), or with something embedded, like a chart's spreadsheet. Of 784 real Word files we tested, 102 were refused, about 1 in 8. #19, #68, #75
  • Excel workbooks with comments, links to other workbooks, pivot tables or database connections. A pivot table can keep a full copy of its source data, even data deleted from every sheet. #76
  • PowerPoint presentations with comments, embedded fonts, or a chart whose spreadsheet is stored inside. That spreadsheet is a whole Excel file with its own author. #78
  • Signed or locked files: PDFs and programs signed by their maker, encrypted PDFs, and e-books and videos with copy protection. Changing them breaks the signature, or needs a key we don't have. #15, #39, #52, #61
  • Videos with subtitles, unless you ask us to drop them. A drone's GPS and a film's subtitles look the same from inside the file. Streaming-style videos are refused too. #39, #65
  • Camera RAW photos from less common makers: Pentax, Leica, Hasselblad and Sigma. #46
  • Archives we can't fully read: password-protected or very large ZIP files, or ones holding a file type we don't clean. 9 of the 42 archives that come with macOS are refused this way. #59
  • Rare versions of common formats: old audio named .mp3, TIFF files over 4 GB, macOS's changing wallpapers, unusual BMP and SVG files, e-books holding two versions of the book, and PDFs with attachments. #3, #15, #56, #57, #61, #67, #72
  • Parts of programs that are not finished programs: compiler leftovers, crash dumps and debug files. #51
  • Files that need more memory than the computer has free. The tool checks first, says both numbers and writes nothing; a helper program that runs too long is stopped the same way. Huge pictures get the light clean only. #38, #83, #84, #85

Things we leave in on purpose

These stay because removing them would break the file or change what it shows. The ones at the top come closest to pointing at a person or a machine.

  • A scrambled block in Nikon RAW photos. Nikon scrambles some colour data with a key made from the camera's serial number. We remove the serial number, but the scrambled block still depends on it. #47
  • Camera make, model and lens in RAW photos. Photo editors need them to show the right colours. Serial numbers, owner names, dates and GPS are removed. #45
  • Folder-name length in programs. We wipe a program's debug information but keep its space. The size of that space hints at how long the build folder's name was. A very short Mac program name stays in its signature. #49, #53
  • Screen or printer size in Word drawings. The drawing is measured in that device's units. It could link two drawings to the same machine. #70
  • Speaker notes, hidden slides and cropped-away picture parts in PowerPoint. They are content the author made, so they stay. The report counts them, because people often forget a deck still carries them. #79
  • Hidden sheets, rows and columns in Excel, and the Excel version number. Formulas may use the hidden cells, so they stay. The report counts them. #77
  • Bookmark names and links in Word. A table of contents needs them to work. We list them so you can check them. #20
  • Text files inside an archive. Notes, CSV files and web pages are kept exactly as written: there is no hidden part to remove. The report lists them. #58
  • A few spare bytes in BMP pictures. Some apps read them, so changing them could change the picture. Someone could hide a little data there. #73
  • How some videos and MP3s were encoded. A video's frame-order table, and an older MP3 encoder header, stay at the light clean. #7, #48
  • The brightness layer and transparency in iPhone photos. They make the photo look right on HDR screens. #32
  • Font and colour-profile names in PDFs. They can show "this was made on a Mac", but not who made it. #14

What cleaning can cost you

The light clean costs almost nothing. The stronger cleans trade something away to hide the app that made the file.

  • Photos and music lose a little quality. A stronger clean re-saves them. Very small files can even get bigger. #4
  • Clean only once. Running the strongest clean on an already-cleaned file loses quality a second time. #29
  • PDFs turned into pictures lose their text. You can no longer search, copy or use a screen reader. And it still doesn't hide the app. #17
  • PDFs get bigger. About a third bigger with the deep clean; the light clean can add a tenth to a PDF that packed its parts together. #18, #40
  • Word's stronger cleans accept all tracked changes and delete comments. The review history is gone. The strongest one may also shift fonts and spacing, and we can't measure how much, because our tests can't drive Word. Even the light clean can move a line by a fraction of a pixel in LibreOffice. #24, #26, #69
  • iPhone photos lose their depth maps. Portrait lighting and background effects stop working. #31
  • Videos lose their timecode and 360-degree motion data. Editing apps can no longer line clips up by time. #66
  • Protected Excel sheets lose their password. The lock stays, but anyone can now remove it. #77
  • Old Mac files lose their resource fork, and a BMP whose colour profile was a file on someone's computer is marked as plain sRGB. #60, #74
  • Large files need memory. The stronger cleans of photos and music need many times the file's size; a 1 GB video needs only 44 MB. The tool checks first and tells you. #38, #83
  • The strongest cleans can show which helper-program versions made them, and for MP3, M4A and PDF which kind of processor (Intel or ARM). Use the container image and everyone on the same kind of processor gets the same output. #88
  • The report shows what it removed. Your name or GPS location appears on screen. You can turn the report off. #28
  • A killed clean can leave a copy of the original for a while, in a folder only your account can open; the next run removes it. #86
  • On a Mac, the system tags every new file. The tag sits beside the file, not inside it, and travels only between Macs. #64

Things we have not tested yet

We don't claim anything we haven't checked. These are open questions, not known leaks.

  • Smarter attacks on MP3 audio. We tested one kind of sound analysis. Research describes a deeper kind we haven't tried. #6
  • Which camera body took a RAW photo. It needs several photos from two cameras of the same model. #47
  • Word's strongest clean, opened in Word. Word can't be run by our tests, so the layout cost is unmeasured. #26
  • Removing a video compressor's settings without re-compressing. It looks possible; it is not measured. #36
  • How much of a video's fingerprint we can see. Some clues only show when Apple's own video writer is compared, which runs only on a Mac. Apple's audio encoder is in the same position. #12, #44
  • Videos from drones and Android phones. iPhone videos and GoPro's published clips are tested; DJI and Android clips are not yet.
  • More than a few RAW photos per maker. We checked about one real file for each RAW format.
  • Excel and PowerPoint files saved by Microsoft Office. Our tests use files from LibreOffice and two Python libraries, because Office refused to save when scripted. #82
  • Embedded fonts in Word, and e-books bought from stores. We had no samples.
  • A blind test by someone else. A second person hasn't tried the tool from the guide alone yet.

Every point on this page was measured, not assumed. The numbers in grey are rows of the project's full list of limits (docs/limits.md, 88 entries), where each one is explained with the measurement behind it.
